summary.text: A finite divisibility case analysis shows that for every \(1\le d\le2025\), one of the prime pairs \((11,13),(7,19),(5,29),(3,17),(2,17)\) has neither prime dividing \(d\); each pair has distinct final digits and product at most \(150\). Since \(d\) is then invertible modulo \(pq\), some \(0\le i<pq\le150\) satisfies \(a+id\equiv0\pmod{pq}\), so that term has prime divisors with two different final digits.

full_proof.text:
Let us call a positive integer lopsided if all of its prime divisors have the same final decimal digit. We prove that there do not exist integers \(a\ge 2\) and \(1\le d\le 2025\) for which all the 150 numbers
\[
a,a+d,a+2d,\ldots,a+149d
\]
are lopsided.

The key is to associate to every possible difference \(d\) two small primes \(p,q\) satisfying all of the following:

1. neither \(p\) nor \(q\) divides \(d\);
2. \(p\) and \(q\) have different final decimal digits;
3. \(pq\le 150\).

We use the following ordered list of prime pairs:
\[
(11,13),\qquad (7,19),\qquad (5,29),\qquad (3,17),\qquad (2,17).
\]
Given \(d\), select the pair by the following rule.

- If neither 11 nor 13 divides \(d\), choose \((p,q)=(11,13)\).
- Otherwise, if neither 7 nor 19 divides \(d\), choose \((p,q)=(7,19)\).
- Otherwise, if neither 5 nor 29 divides \(d\), choose \((p,q)=(5,29)\).
- Otherwise, if neither 3 nor 17 divides \(d\), choose \((p,q)=(3,17)\).
- If all four preceding tests fail, choose \((p,q)=(2,17)\).

All numbers occurring in these pairs are prime. The primes within each pair are distinct and have different residues modulo 10. Explicitly, their final digits are respectively
\[
(1,3),\quad (7,9),\quad (5,9),\quad (3,7),\quad (2,7).
\]
Their products are
\[
11\cdot13=143,\quad 7\cdot19=133,\quad 5\cdot29=145,
\quad 3\cdot17=51,\quad 2\cdot17=34,
\]
all at most 150.

It remains to justify in every branch that neither selected prime divides \(d\). This is immediate in each of the first four branches, because the condition defining that branch says exactly that neither member of the selected pair divides \(d\). We therefore examine the last branch.

If the last branch is reached, all four previous tests have failed. Consequently,
\[
11\mid d\ \text{or}\ 13\mid d,
\]
\[
7\mid d\ \text{or}\ 19\mid d,
\]
\[
5\mid d\ \text{or}\ 29\mid d,
\]
and
\[
3\mid d\ \text{or}\ 17\mid d.
\]
We show first that \(2\nmid d\). Suppose instead that \(2\mid d\). Choose a prime
\[
r_1\in\{11,13\},\quad r_2\in\{7,19\},\quad
r_3\in\{5,29\},\quad r_4\in\{3,17\}
\]
which divides \(d\) in each of the four displayed alternatives. The five numbers
\(2,r_1,r_2,r_3,r_4\) are distinct primes. Since each divides \(d\), their product divides \(d\). Because \(d\ge1\), this implies
\[
d\ge 2r_1r_2r_3r_4.
\]
Each chosen prime is at least the smaller member of its indicated pair, and hence
\[
d\ge 2\cdot11\cdot7\cdot5\cdot3=2310,
\]
contrary to \(d\le2025\). Thus \(2\nmid d\).

Next we show that \(17\nmid d\). If \(17\mid d\), choose divisors
\[
r_1\in\{11,13\},\qquad r_2\in\{7,19\},\qquad
r_3\in\{5,29\}
\]
using the failure of the first three tests. The four numbers \(17,r_1,r_2,r_3\) are distinct primes, so their product divides \(d\). Again using \(d>0\),
\[
d\ge17r_1r_2r_3\ge17\cdot11\cdot7\cdot5=6545,
\]
which is again impossible because \(d\le2025\). Therefore \(17\nmid d\). This proves that the pair \((2,17)\) also has the required nondivisibility property in the final branch.

We have therefore established that for every integer \(d\) with \(1\le d\le2025\), the rule supplies primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
p\nmid d,\qquad q\nmid d,\qquad p\not\equiv q\pmod {10},
\qquad pq\le150.
\]

Now suppose, toward a contradiction, that some \(a\ge2\) and \(1\le d\le2025\) give 150 lopsided terms \(a+id\), \(0\le i<150\). Choose \(p,q\) for this \(d\) as above.

Because \(p\) and \(q\) are distinct primes and neither divides \(d\), we have
\[
\gcd(d,pq)=1.
\]
Thus \(d\) has a multiplicative inverse modulo \(pq\). The congruence
\[
a+id\equiv0\pmod{pq}
\]
therefore has a solution modulo \(pq\), namely
\[
i\equiv -a d^{-1}\pmod{pq}.
\]
Take the least nonnegative representative of this residue class. Then
\[
0\le i<pq\le150,
\]
so \(i\) is one of the allowed indices \(0,1,\ldots,149\). By its construction,
\[
pq\mid a+id.
\]
In particular, both \(p\) and \(q\) divide \(a+id\).

The number \(a+id\) is positive, since \(a\ge2\), \(i\ge0\), and \(d\ge1\). Hence the prime divisors \(p\) and \(q\) genuinely occur among its prime factors. But
\[
p\not\equiv q\pmod {10},
\]
so these two prime divisors have different final decimal digits. Therefore \(a+id\) is not lopsided, contradicting the assumption that every one of the 150 progression terms is lopsided.

This contradiction applies to every possible \(a\ge2\) and every \(d\) with \(1\le d\le2025\). Consequently, no increasing arithmetic progression of 150 terms with difference at most 2025 can consist entirely of numbers whose prime divisors share the same final decimal digit. Thus the stated existential conjecture is false.
